messages.text:
You are an implementation subagent for the research agent "claude". claude is building an in-house WSA-like coronal model plus 3D MHD heliosphere to estimate the solar-wind flux at interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS on 2025-12-03/04, when the comet was at about 1.88 AU near the ecliptic. Plasma reaching the comet left the Sun around 2025-11-20 to 2025-11-30. Your job is the CORONAL MODEL: photospheric magnetogram → PFSS → WSA-type empirical speed → inner-boundary maps at 0.1 AU (21.5 R_sun) for the heliospheric MHD code that claude is writing in CUDA. Work fully autonomously: no human will answer questions. Make the scientific calls, justify them in the README, and report them.

WORKSPACE (write only here): code in /mnt/c/Users/cabot/OneDrive/Documents/Research/Cambridge/X3I/mhd_llm/claude/src/corona/, outputs in mhd_llm/claude/data/boundary/, QC in mhd_llm/claude/data/boundary/qc/. Never write to mhd_llm/argon, mhd_llm/codex, or mhd_llm/shared_notes. Another subagent is concurrently downloading GONG mrzqs and ADAPT-GONG maps into mhd_llm/claude/data/gong/ and data/adapt/ (with index.csv files) and writing a WSA/ENLIL/EUHFORIA boundary-prescription memo to data/remote_sensing_memo.md. Don't wait for it to start: download one or two GONG mrzqs maps yourself from https://gong.nso.edu/data/magmap/ (QR zero-corrected synoptic, mrzqs, near 2025-11-25) into src/corona/devmaps/ for development, then switch to the shared data/gong/ files when they appear. The CCMC reference run used WSA v5.4 + GONGz with ENLIL a6b1 (vfast=700, vslow=200, vrfast=25, vrslow=75 km/s, bfast=350 nT, bscl=4, dfast=125 cm^-3, tfast=1.5 MK); its control file is mhd_llm/claude/ref/ccmc/Jan_Deca_120925_SH_1_control_file.txt.

RESOURCES: shared machine. Use at most 8 CPU threads, at most 4 GB RAM, and no GPU (the GPU is reserved for the MHD code). Wrap runs in `systemd-run --user --scope --quiet -p MemoryMax=4G ...`. Prefer C++17 with OpenMP (g++ 13.3) for field-line tracing and anything hot, with Python driving it. Python: /home/scabot/miniconda3/bin/python3 (numpy, scipy, astropy, matplotlib), or /home/scabot/miniconda3/envs/mhd_claude/bin/python (adds numba, sunpy, h5py; it is being built now, so check whether it exists). Do not install packages into the base env. Parse downloaded FITS with `python -I`. Test at low resolution first and keep each run fast (target under 1 min per map end to end).

CODE STYLE (user mandate): parsimonious and well-structured, with NO comments and NO docstrings in code, and no free-text note fields in output JSON. Explanations go in src/corona/README.md. American spelling.

SPECIFICATION
1. Read GONG mrzqs (360×180, sine-latitude grid, Gauss; get the Carrington longitude convention and map time from the header, e.g. CAR_ROT, CRVAL1, LONGITUDE of the map's leading edge) and ADAPT-GONG (lat grid, 12 realizations; pick realization via argument). Remove the monopole. Optionally apply polar filling/smoothing; document it.
2. PFSS via spherical-harmonic expansion with source surface Rss=2.5 R_sun (configurable) and lmax configurable (default 60–90, with a convergence check). Validate against an analytic dipole PFSS solution: report the max relative error in B on a test grid.
3. Field-line tracing (C++/OpenMP, RK4 or adaptive RK45, analytic SH field evaluation or interpolation from a gridded field cube; make sure it's fast). For every pixel of a 1°×1° Carrington grid on the source surface (or on a finer grid, then average), trace down to the photosphere: get the expansion factor f_s = (R_sun/R_ss)^2 · |B(R_sun)|/|B(R_ss)| and the footpoint. Build the photospheric open-field (coronal hole) mask by tracing up from a photospheric grid. Compute θ_b, the great-circle angular distance from each footpoint to the nearest coronal-hole boundary (use a fast distance transform on the sphere or a KD-tree on boundary points).
4. WSA speed, with configurable coefficients: v = v0 + v1 / (1+f_s)^a · (1 − 0.8·exp(−(θ_b/w)^b))^c. Default to the WSA v5.x / ENLIL-coupled values from the literature (e.g. Arge et al. 2003/2004, McGregor et al. 2011, Riley et al. 2015, Reiss et al. 2019); check data/remote_sensing_memo.md when it appears, and record exactly which values you adopt and why. Note that WSA's v is a terminal (≈1 AU) speed: implement the ENLIL-style reduction at 0.1 AU (vr_inner = v − Δ with Δ interpolated between vrslow=75 at slow and vrfast=25 at fast; check Odstrcil's documented a6b1 rule) and also a EUHFORIA-style option (v − 50 km/s, capped). Plasma at the inner boundary: ENLIL-like n = dfast·(vfast/v)^2 (momentum-flux balance), T = tfast·(n_fast/n) (thermal-pressure balance), B_r = sign(B_ss polarity)·bfast·(v/vfast)?? Verify the actual ENLIL rule. EUHFORIA uses B_r = sgn(B_ss)·B_fsw·(v/v_fsw) and n v^2 = const. Implement the documented rules of both models as options, and make the mapping from source surface to 21.5 R_sun explicit (radial, or a Schatten current-sheet model if you have time; radial is acceptable to leading order, so document it).
5. Output, per input map time: data/boundary/<source>_<YYYYMMDDTHHMM>[_r<NN>].npz with arrays lon_carr_deg (0.5..359.5, 1° centers), lat_deg (-89.5..89.5), v_wsa_kms (terminal), vr_kms (at 0.1 AU), n_cm3, T_K, br_nT (at 0.1 AU), fs, thetab_deg, polarity, open_mask_photosphere (if useful), and scalar metadata (map time UTC, Carrington rotation and longitude convention, coefficients). Also write data/boundary/index.csv. Then produce maps for every daily GONG mrzqs map from 2025-11-01 to 2025-12-04 (and ADAPT realizations, if downloaded, for the same dates, at least 3 realizations, preferably 12) once the downloads exist.
6. Validation QC (PNGs in data/boundary/qc/): source-surface Br with neutral line; photospheric open-field mask over the magnetogram; f_s, θ_b, and v_wsa maps for 2025-11-25; and a quick 1-D ballistic check. Take the WSA terminal speed at the sub-Earth heliographic latitude, map it ballistically (constant speed, with the Carrington longitude shift for 1 AU travel) to Earth for Nov 10–Dec 10 2025, and compare with OMNI hourly speed (fetch OMNI2_H0_MRG1HR V from https://cdaweb.gsfc.nasa.gov/hapi if data/insitu/hourly_omni*.csv doesn't exist yet). Report correlation and RMSE, and do the same for STEREO-A if its data are available (data/insitu/ or the preprint cache at /mnt/c/Users/cabot/OneDrive/Documents/Research/Cambridge/X3I/analysis_repro/analysis_06_solar_wind/cache/stereo_a.csv: columns time, speed, density). For geometry, use sub-observer Carrington longitude and latitude from sunpy or a simple ephemeris; data/ephem/ will hold Horizons-based files with carr_lon_deg and carr_lat_deg columns when the other subagent finishes.
7. src/corona/README.md: method, equations, adopted coefficients with citations, validation numbers, run time per map, and how to call it (CLI and Python function signature).

FINAL REPLY (compact): files and CLI usage; validation numbers (dipole PFSS error, lmax convergence, OMNI and STEREO-A ballistic correlation/RMSE); adopted coefficients and boundary rules; timing per map; open issues.

<system-reminder>
Your final report is delivered through SubagentHandback: when your work is complete, call SubagentHandback({message: <your full report>}). The call ends your run, so make it your last step. Only a SubagentHandback call reaches your caller as your result; plain text you write at the end is not delivered. Do not also send the report with SendMessage: your caller would get it twice.
</system-reminder>
The local log contains an empty or redacted thinking block; plaintext is unavailable.

You are an expert astrophysicist --- a widely recognized authority on high-energy processes, magnetohydrodynamics (MHD), and cutting-edge numerical methods. You write code which is well-structured, parsimonious, and highly optimized for the compute systems at hand. You are highly skeptical of your own results, and constructively critical of the claims made by both published literature and your own collaborators. You are tasked with the following project: BACKGROUND: The first X-ray detection of an interstellar object was announced in December 2025, involving a single ~80 kilosecond XMM-Newton/EPIC observation of 3I/ATLAS at approximately 1.8 AU from the Earth and Sun. 3I/ATLAS is remarkable for its interstellar provenance, distinctive coma chemistry, and potentially 10+ Gyr old age. The X-ray signature is from solar-wind charge exchange: an interaction whereby the neutral coma sublimated from the comet nucleus donates electrons to heavy ions in the solar wind. The preprint of a research paper, presenting the X-ray detection, is available for your review at: /mnt/c/Users/cabot/OneDrive/Documents/Research/Cambridge/X3I/Drafts/20260830_submission The repository for data reduction and analysis is available at the following path: /mnt/c/Users/cabot/OneDrive/Documents/Research/Cambridge/X3I/analysis_repro The X-ray surface brightness depends on the column density of the neutral medium and the flux of incident heavy ions. It has weak dependence on the composition of the neutral gas. The X-ray spectrum depends on the solar wind composition, and is typically dominated by H- or He-like carbon, oxygen, and nitrogen ions. It is impossible to know the precise speed and composition of the solar wind at the both the location of 3I/ATLAS and at the observed epoch. The preprint analyzes publicly available proton flux timeseries data from multiple remote sensing solar wind probes, and approximates the local solar wind properties using a crude Parker Spiral extrapolation. This approach disregards, for example, azimuthal heterogeneities, and the fact that fast wind may overtake slow wind. A more comprehensive modeling of the solar wind was requested by an external reviewer. They recommended the model here be taken into consideration: https://ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/ror/results/viewrun.php?runnumber=Jan_Deca_120925_SH_1 However, an in-house implementation will allow a more bespoke analysis, tailored to this specific project. GOAL: Implement a 3D MHD simulation of the solar wind, and use it to model the incident flux at 3I/ATLAS during the XMM-Newton epoch. Ensure that the model accounts for available remote sensing observations of both the Sun and the solar wind. Conduct research on which remote sensing products are most relevant. The final products should include (1) an estimate timeseries of the proton and/or heavy-ion number density and speed at 3I/ATLAS during the observation plotted as 1D charts (time versus density, time versus speed, time versus flux); and (2) a 2D top-down animation of the inner Solar System showing the propagation of the solar wind from the Sun out to at least 2 AU (colormap corresponding to solar wind flux). Keep the analysis tractable. Use only the inputs that affect final results to the leading orders. Perform tests and initial experiments at intentionally low resolution and short runtimes in order to rapidly iterate on code. Be intentionally conservative regarding consumed resources (especially memory and runtime). Your code should be hyper-optimized, possibly in C++ and/or CUDA, to make extremely efficient use of the resources available on this machine. The machine must never stall out. Design benchmarks for your analysis, including but not limited to: replication of literature simulation results; replication of trends observed in empirical datasets; calibration to the remote sensing data using the preprint; comparison against the above CCMC NASA model. Demonstrate convergence in your results (i.e., increased spatial or temporal resolution, or additional physics, would not yield substantial accuracy improvements). PARAMETERS: Your work, excluding external dependencies such as python environments or other third-party software, will be fully self-contained at: /mnt/c/Users/cabot/OneDrive/Documents/Research/Cambridge/X3I/mhd_llm/claude Use sub-agents liberally in order to conduct research and parallelize implementation or analysis tasks. Your work will be your own. You are responsible for your final results. However, you will work collaboratively with other research agents. You will record your progress, intermediate results, and any important insights (which may be astrophysical in nature or simply related to coding on this machine) via timestamped and consistently formatted notes. These notes clearly must clearly establish your unique identity as the authoring agent. They should be placed at: /mnt/c/Users/cabot/OneDrive/Documents/Research/Cambridge/X3I/mhd_llm/shared_notes You are welcome to read the notes created by other models, including direct communication with those models through questions and answers placed in this note exchange directory. You will work autonomously until this project is complete and the mandated visualizations are created. No further questions will be answered from the human user. The human user will not be available to run commands, so you must understand and work within your own permissions scoping. Finally, you will use monitor tasks to maintain the following: 1. a record of total runtime of the project so far 2. a record of compute usage statistics, as available 3. a record of tokens consumed on the project 4. an estimate of project completion 4. checks for new notes from collaborators Proceed. ---- # ENLIL v2.8f control file draft # # ALL NULL ARGS ARE NOT PASSED ON # # uploaded CME parameters file name is DONKI_2025-09-01_2025-12-09_v600_w30.txt # batch=yes # Submit run to batch queue project=Jan_Deca_120925_SH_1 # Use run request number for project directory name *RUNID* cr=null # Carrington Rotation number (null | xxxx) (null for du and dt run types) reg=3 # Computational region res=low # Numerical grid resolution nblk=2 # Number of computational blocks (1 for ambient run, 2 for CME run) vutime=null # Time unit scale factor (s) gives default 3600. The search didn't turn up the exact vfast/vslow/bfast/dfast/tfast formulas. It did confirm the general inner-boundary scheme and that the variables are used for scaling or clipping WSA values.

- **Boundary location and variables:** The WSA-derived solution is handed to ENLIL at 21.5 solar radii, where the time-dependent boundary conditions are built from the WSA output and CME parameters. The MHD domain runs from 21.5 solar radii to just beyond Earth's orbit, while the inner portion from the photosphere to 21.5 R_s is characterized by WSA.
- **Density and temperature:** Density and temperature are specified from the assumptions of constant momentum flux and thermal pressure balance along a flux tube, respectively. A comparative study describes the same approach for the MAS/ENLIL coupling. The proton density is derived from momentum-flux balance, and plasma temperature is calculated under the assumption of thermal-pressure balance at the inner radial boundary.
- **Magnetic field:** The radial component of the magnetic field is used directly from the coronal model. The meridional component is assumed to be zero, and the azimuthal component is derived from the rotation speed of the source surface.
- **Velocity variables:** One NASA/NOAA annex report notes that Eric Adamson has been investigating differences between the different ENLIL versions in how the variables vfast, bfast, dfast, and tfast are used for scaling and/or clipping WSA values. That is the only source I found that names these variables, and it gives no formulas.
- **Temperature assumption:** Enlil commonly assumes equal electron and proton temperatures at the inner boundary.

For the actual vfast/vslow mapping and the bfast/dfast/tfast scaling rules, the next step would be the ENLIL source code or its documentation, or the arXiv 2512.14462 annex report, which may contain the details.
